title: Practice online
hookLine: a man hurls insults at the Buddha, who asks whose food it is when guests refuse it: right speech in the comment section
tomorrow: why did a rich tax collector climb a tree to see Jesus?

cards: A post, a reply, a reply to the reply, and ten comments later strangers are calling each other names. The Pali texts have a man like that.
Akkosaka Bharadvaja hears that a man of his clan has become a monk under the Buddha. He's furious. He goes straight to the Buddha and lets him have it: insult after insult, rude and harsh.
The Buddha waits until he's finished. Then he asks him a question about guests.

teach.b: Do friends and relatives ever visit you? Sometimes, the man says. Do you offer them food?
Sometimes. And if they don't accept it, whose is it? Then it's mine.
In the same way, the Buddha says, I don't accept your abuse. It's all yours. The sutta ends with the man going forth as a monk himself.

teach.h: RIGHT SPEECH: FOUR THINGS NOT SENT.
teach.b: Under the story sits the Buddhist teaching of right speech, one part of the Noble Eightfold Path: refraining from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech and idle chatter.

teach.h: THE FOOD STAYS ON THE TABLE.

teach.b: Right speech is what you don't send. And the Buddha's reply shows what you don't have to take. Online, that's most of the practice.
Before you post: is it true, does it divide, is it harsh, is it worth saying? And when a hostile reply lands, the food can stay on the table.

how: Buddhists learn right speech as part of the Noble Eightfold Path, and those who take the five precepts keep one against false speech. Teachers tell the story of the refused gift of abuse to show that insults need not be taken up.

o: logging off social media for good
careful, kind speech in the comments

p: came to hurl insults at the Buddha
stays with the one who offered it
nothing false, divisive, harsh or idle

s: right speech means never disagreeing with anyone
it rules out false, divisive, harsh and idle words, not honest disagreement.
in the story, the Buddha answers the insults with a sharp comeback
he asks about refused food: whose is it? the abuse stays with the one who brought it.
the angry man in the story later became a monk himself
the sutta says he went forth under the Buddha.

games.q: someone quote-posts you with a mean, half-true jab, and your friends are watching to see what you'll do. which fits right speech?
o: correct the false part once, calmly, and leave the jab alone
never post again, since anything online is idle chatter
match their tone so nobody thinks you're weak
games.why: right speech still says what's true. it refuses harsh and divisive words, and the Buddha's reply shows the insult can stay with its sender.

practice: Open a message or a comment you've meant to write, and version one kind line. Run it past the four: true, not dividing, not harsh, worth saying.
Then set the phone face down and breathe with the version unsent until the sit is done.

wordCard.voice: Practice online: right speech in the comments. Nothing false, divisive, harsh or idle sent, and insults left unaccepted, like refused food.

orig.note: Pali: right speech, one part of the Noble Eightfold Path.

carryVoice: Your line: right speech online. The Buddha left the insult with the one who brought it. That's the week, day 1729.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 7.2, Akkosa Sutta (Akkosaka Bharadvaja reviles the Buddha; the food guests refuse; he later goes forth)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.8 (right speech: abstaining from false, divisive, harsh speech and idle chatter)
